content:
Your church's employee records include identity information, wage records and tax forms. Federal agencies give these records different retention rules, so the date someone leaves does not start the same clock for every document.

Use this reference to distinguish the forms you retain, the records behind payroll and the files that need restricted access. Apply each federal rule only where it covers your church and the employee's work.

---

## Check which rules apply

The Department of Labor distinguishes FLSA enterprise coverage from individual employee coverage. A nonprofit's charitable or religious activities do not themselves establish enterprise coverage, but an employee may still have individual coverage through interstate work. Check coverage before applying the wage-record rules below.

EEOC coverage also varies by the law and type of employer. Its retention rules apply to covered employers. Use the applicable agency's coverage guidance rather than assuming every federal employment rule has the same reach.

<Callout type="important">
Federal guidance checked October 16, 2026. Confirm current forms and retention instructions with USCIS, the Department of Labor, the IRS and the EEOC before using this reference to dispose of records. The periods below address different record categories and do not replace one another.
</Callout>

---

## Keep the hiring forms

Form I-9 documents verification of a new employee's identity and authorization to work in the United States. The employee completes and signs Section 1 no later than the first day of employment. Complete Section 2 within three business days after that first day. If employment will last less than three business days, complete Section 2 no later than the first day.

Provide the I-9 instructions and Lists of Acceptable Documents. Let the employee choose acceptable documentation. Retain the completed form rather than mailing it to USCIS or ICE.

For employees subject to federal income-tax withholding, ask for a signed Form W-4 when work starts and apply it to the first wage payment. Keep withholding certificates among the employment-tax records. Use the related payroll article for the separate review of clergy tax treatment.

---

## Calculate the I-9 retention date

USCIS requires you to keep the completed I-9 and its attachments throughout employment. Once employment ends, retain them until the later of these dates:

- Three years after the first day of employment.
- One year from the date employment ends.

Compare both dates before deciding that the retention period has ended. Do not discard a current employee's form merely because three years have passed since hiring.

Retain supplement pages containing entered information and any photocopies you made of the employee's documentation. The instructions do not require you to retain unused instructions or Lists of Acceptable Documents pages.

<Callout type="tip">
USCIS says completed I-9s and accompanying documents should be stored in a safe, secure location. Electronic generation, signing and retention are permitted when they comply with DHS regulations. A scan alone does not establish that the electronic system meets those standards.
</Callout>

---

## Preserve the wage calculation

For covered nonexempt workers, DOL Fact Sheet 21 calls for accurate identifying information and records of hours worked and wages earned. No particular record form is required.

The basic records include the employee's full name, Social Security number, address, sex and occupation, plus birth date if younger than 19. Record when the workweek begins, daily and weekly hours, pay basis, regular hourly rate, straight-time and overtime earnings, additions and deductions, total pay, payment date and pay period.

| FLSA record category | DOL retention guidance |
|---|---|
| Payroll records, collective bargaining agreements, sales and purchase records | Preserve for at least three years. |
| Records used to calculate wages, including time cards, wage-rate tables, work schedules and additions or deductions | Retain for two years. |

Any timekeeping method is acceptable if complete and accurate. If you use a fixed schedule and the employee works longer or shorter hours, record the actual hours worked. Keep the records available for DOL inspection.

---

## Retain the employment-tax support

The IRS employment-tax recordkeeping page says to keep these records for at least four years after filing the fourth quarter for the year. This is a tax-record rule, separate from the FLSA periods above.

The IRS list includes:

- The church's EIN and employees' names, addresses, Social Security numbers and occupations.
- Employment dates, wage amounts and payment dates.
- Withholding certificates, including Forms W-4.
- Tax-deposit dates, amounts and EFTPS acknowledgment numbers.
- Copies of filed returns and confirmation numbers.
- Fringe-benefit and expense-reimbursement records, including substantiation.
- Employee copies of Forms W-2 and W-2c returned as undeliverable.

The same IRS page identifies longer retention for certain tax-credit records. Check the credit-specific instructions if those records are in your files, rather than applying the ordinary period to every tax document.

---

## Retain personnel and applicant records

The EEOC's Part 1602 summary covers personnel and employment records that covered entities make or use. Examples include applications, accommodation requests, hiring and termination records, pay decisions and training selections.

For covered private employers, retain these records for one year from creation or the personnel action involved, whichever is later. For an involuntary termination, keep the terminated employee's personnel or employment records for one year from termination. The summary gives educational institutions a different period, so a church operating a school should check that category separately.

EEOC guidance also identifies three-year payroll retention under the ADEA, where applicable. Keep employee benefit plans and written seniority or merit systems for their full effective period and at least one year after termination under those requirements.

<Callout type="warning">
An EEOC discrimination charge changes the disposal decision. Preserve relevant personnel or employment records until final disposition of the charge or any lawsuit based on it, including appeals. An ordinary retention date does not override that requirement.
</Callout>

---

## Separate confidential medical information

Under the ADA's confidentiality rules, medical information belongs on separate forms and in separate medical files. The EEOC says not to place medical material in the regular personnel file. That confidentiality obligation continues after the person is no longer an applicant or employee.

For personal information generally, follow the FTC's practical security guidance. Limit access to what each person's job needs. Keep sensitive paper files and backups in a locked room or cabinet. Inventory electronic copies and outside service providers as well as the main filing cabinet.

Use Social Security numbers only for required and lawful purposes. Do not reuse them as routine employee identification numbers.

---

## Check before closing a file

Use these checks when employment ends or records reach a review date:

- [ ] Confirm the employment end date and compare both I-9 retention dates.
- [ ] Check the applicable wage, tax and personnel-record periods separately.
- [ ] Preserve records subject to an EEOC charge or related lawsuit through final disposition.
- [ ] Keep medical information separate and confidential after departure.
- [ ] Review who still needs access to sensitive files.
- [ ] When retention needs end, dispose of sensitive paper and electronic records securely, following the FTC's guidance.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"But all things must be done properly and in an orderly manner."* — 1 Corinthians 14:40 (LSB)
</Callout>
excerpt: Keep church employee forms and records with precise federal retention periods, confidential storage and checks before disposal.
title: HR Records and Required Forms

sources.claim: Opening and hiring forms: I-9 purpose; first-day Section 1; Section 2 three business days after first day, with short-employment exception.
sources.quote:
The form is used to document verification of the identity and employment authorization of each new employee (both U.S. citizen and alien) hired after November 6, 1986, to work in the United States.
Employees must complete and sign Section 1 of Form I-9 no later than the first day of employment
Complete Section 2 within three business days after the employee's first day of employment. If you hire an individual for less than three business days, complete Section 2 no later than the first day of employment.

sources.claim: Hiring forms: provide instructions and lists; employee chooses; retain rather than mail.
sources.quote:
Employers must allow all employees to choose which acceptable documentation to present for Form I-9.
Make the instructions for Form I-9 and Lists of Acceptable Documents available to the employee
Retain completed forms. You are not required to retain or store the page(s) containing the Lists of Acceptable Documents or the instructions for Form I-9. Do not mail completed forms to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) or Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

sources.claim: I-9 retention and closing checklist: keep throughout employment, attachments and later-of date comparison.
sources.quote: An employer must retain Form I-9, including any supplement pages, on which the employee and employer (or authorized representative) entered data, as well as any photocopies made of the documentation the employee presented, for as long as the employee works for the employer. When employment ends, the employer must retain the individual's Form I-9 and all attachments for one year from the date employment ends, or three years after the first day of employment, whichever is later.

sources.claim: I-9 secure storage and electronic-retention callout; current-form reminder.
sources.quote:
Completed Forms I-9 and all accompanying documents should be stored in a safe and secure location.
Form I-9 may be generated, signed, and retained electronically, in compliance with Department of Homeland Security regulations at 8 CFR section 274a.2.
To ensure you are using the latest version of this form and corresponding instructions, visit the USCIS website at www.uscis.gov/i-9.

sources.claim: Coverage: charitable/religious activities do not themselves establish enterprise coverage; individual interstate-work coverage may apply. No nonprofit-wide exemption asserted.
sources.quote:
There are two ways in which an employee can be covered by the law and therefore entitled to its protections: “enterprise coverage” and “individual coverage.”
Charitable, religious, educational, or similar activities of organizations operated on a non-profit basis where such activities are not in substantial competition with other businesses do not result in the organizations being considered covered enterprises.
Employees of employers that are not covered by the FLSA on an enterprise basis may still be entitled to its protections if they are individually engaged in interstate commerce

sources.claim: Opening, wage-record section: coverage, accuracy, no required form, full identifying and pay data.
sources.quote:
Every covered employer must keep certain records for each non-exempt worker. The Act requires no particular form for the records, but does require that the records include certain identifying information about the employee and data about the hours worked and the wages earned. The law requires this information to be accurate.
Employee's full name and social security number.
Address, including zip code.
Birth date, if younger than 19.
Sex and occupation.
Time and day of week when employee's workweek begins.
Hours worked each day.
Total hours worked each workweek.
Basis on which employee's wages are paid
Regular hourly pay rate.
Total daily or weekly straight-time earnings.
Total overtime earnings for the workweek.
All additions to or deductions from the employee's wages.
Total wages paid each pay period.
Date of payment and the pay period covered by the payment.

sources.claim: Wage retention table, timekeeping, actual hours on schedule exceptions and inspection; closing checklist wage check.
sources.quote:
Each employer shall preserve for at least three years payroll records, collective bargaining agreements, sales and purchase records. Records on which wage computations are based should be retained for two years, i.e., time cards and piece work tickets, wage rate tables, work and time schedules, and records of additions to or deductions from wages. These records must be open for inspection by the Division's representatives
Any timekeeping plan is acceptable as long as it is complete and accurate.
When a worker is on a job for a longer or shorter period of time than the schedule shows, the employer must record the number of hours the worker actually worked, on an exception basis.

sources.claim: Coverage caution for EEOC laws; no universal employee threshold asserted.
sources.quote:
An employer must have a certain number of employees to be covered by the laws we enforce.
This number varies depending on the type of employer

sources.claim: W-4 timing for employees subject to withholding; clergy payroll referred to published related article.
sources.quote: Ask all new employees to give you a signed Form W-4 when they start work. Make the form effective with the first wage payment.

sources.claim: Tax section and closing checklist: ordinary retention starts after fourth-quarter filing; special tax-credit records have longer periods.
sources.quote:
Keep all records of employment taxes for at least four years after filing the 4th quarter for the year. These should be available for IRS review.
Documentation to substantiate any credits claimed. Records related to qualified sick leave wages and qualified family leave wages for leave taken after March 31, 2021, and records related to qualified wages for the employee retention credit paid after June 30, 2021, should be kept for at least 6 years.

sources.claim: Tax-record checklist and opening: identifying data, wages, certificates, deposits, returns, fringe benefits, reimbursements and returned W-2/W-2c employee copies.
sources.quote:
Your employer identification number.
Amounts and dates of all wage, annuity, and pension payments.
Names, addresses, social security numbers, and occupations of employees and recipients.
Any employee copies of Form W-2 and W-2c returned to you as undeliverable.
Dates of employment for each employee.
Copies of employees' and recipients' income tax withholding certificates (Forms W-4, W-4P, W-4S, and W-4V).
Dates and amounts of tax deposits you made and acknowledgment numbers for deposits made by EFTPS.
Copies of returns filed and confirmation numbers.
Records of fringe benefits and expenses reimbursements provided to your employees, including substantiation.

sources.claim: Personnel/applicant section: made-or-used records and examples; private-employer later-of one-year rule; involuntary termination rule; educational institutions separate category.
sources.quote:
These recordkeeping regulations require covered entities to retain personnel and employment records that they make or use in the course of their business.
All Personnel and Employment Records made or used (including, but not limited to, requests for reasonable accommodation, application forms submitted by applicants, and records dealing with hiring, promotion, demotion, transfer, lay-off or termination, rates of pay, compensation, tenure, selection for training or apprenticeship, or other terms of employment)
Private employers must retain such records for one year from the date of making the record or the personnel action involved, whichever occurs later, but in the case of involuntary termination of an employee, they must retain the terminated employee's personnel or employment records for one year from the date of termination.
Educational Institutions and State and Local Governments must retain such records for two years from the date of the making of the record or the personnel action involved, whichever occurs later

sources.claim: ADEA paragraph: payroll, employee benefit plans, written seniority/merit systems and applicable coverage.
sources.quote:
Under ADEA recordkeeping requirements, employers must also keep all payroll records for three years. Additionally, employers must keep on file any employee benefit plan (such as pension and insurance plans) and any written seniority or merit system for the full period the plan or system is in effect and for at least one year after its termination.
These requirements apply to all employers covered by Federal anti-discrimination laws, regardless of whether a charge has been filed against the employer.

sources.claim: Warning and closing checklist: relevant charge records through final disposition including appeals.
sources.quote:
Once a charge is filed, these records must be kept until the final disposition of the charge or any lawsuit based on the charge.
where suit is brought by the charging party or the EEOC, the date on which the litigation is terminated, including any appeals.

sources.claim: Medical files section and departure checklist: separate forms/files, regular personnel file exclusion and continuing confidentiality.
sources.quote:
Medical information must be collected and maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files.
An employer should not place any medical-related material in an employee's non-medical personnel file.
Does the confidentiality obligation end when the person is no longer an applicant or employee?
No, an employer must keep medical information confidential even if someone is no longer an applicant (for example, s/he wasn't hired) or is no longer an employee.

sources.claim: Opening organizational suggestions, confidential-files practical guidance, limited access, inventory across electronic copies/providers, SSN use, closing access review and secure disposal.
sources.quote:
Inventory all computers, laptops, mobile devices, flash drives, disks, home computers, digital copiers, and other equipment to find out where your company stores sensitive data.
Track personal information through your business by talking with your sales department, information technology staff, human resources office, accounting personnel, and outside service providers.
Scale down access to data. Follow the “principle of least privilege.” That means each employee should have access only to those resources needed to do their particular job.
Store paper documents or files, as well as thumb drives and backups containing personally identifiable information in a locked room or in a locked file cabinet. Limit access to employees with a legitimate business need.
Use Social Security numbers only for required and lawful purposes— like reporting employee taxes. Don’t use Social Security numbers unnecessarily—for example, as an employee or customer identification number, or because you’ve always done it.
If you must keep information for business reasons or to comply with the law, develop a written records retention policy to identify what information must be kept, how to secure it, how long to keep it, and how to dispose of it securely when you no longer need it.

claim_check.notes: Author opened primary sources; independent Opus sentence-by-sentence, scripture and desktop/mobile review required. USCIS PDF and DOL fact sheets were fetched directly when the web reader failed.

rulings: Mechanics only. Employment-policy content, religious hiring preferences and ministerial-exception analysis are outside A27.
Federal coverage remains conditional; no single retention period is presented for an entire employee file. No state example is needed.

Use the IRS employment-tax page fourth-quarter filing trigger, consistent with the published corporate-records article. Tax-credit exceptions are signposted without adding historical credit deadlines.
The closing checklist is an editorial recap of the sourced mechanics, not an employment policy. FTC practices are identified as practical guidance.
